To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the year-to-year variations of the terrestrial (CO2)-13C/(12)CO2 exchange are too low to account for the observed atmospheric (CO2)-12C/(13)CO2 variations, and (2) the disequilibrium flux, the return flux of (13)C from the biospheric pools to the atmosphere, has a much lower year-to-year variability than the atmospheric (CO2)-(13)C/(12)C variations.
the IAV in the disequilibrium flux from the terrestrial biosphere is much smaller than previously assumed and that the C-13 budget of the terrestrial biosphere needs to be further improved.

the year-to-year variations of the isotopic disequilbrium flux of the terrestrial biosphere are much less than required to close the atmospheric carbon-13 budget, suggesting that other carbon-13 budget terms must have significantly different interannual variabilities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of terrestrial biosphere processes in explaining the observed atmospheric C(13)IAV and shows that this role is not straightforward to quantify.
the question of whether the observed atmospheric C(13)-C-12 variations are dominated by IAV in biospheric exchange, and our results suggest that this is unlikely to be the case.
the question of how to best partition the total terrestrial carbon sink into its components, and how to quantify their interannual variability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the terrestrial biosphere is not the main cause of atmospheric C-13 variability on an interannual time scale.
the terrestrial C-13 disequilibrium flux does not significantly contribute to the observed C-13 IAV in atmospheric CO2.
the atmospheric C-12 and 13 budgets are still not fully understood, which is a major obstacle for accurate partitioning of the global carbon sink.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
SiBCASA does not reproduce the observed atmospheric IAV in C-13, but that the model is still a useful tool for studying terrestrial C-13 fluxes.
the IAV in terrestrial C-13 exchange is not large enough to explain the observed atmospheric C(13)IAV.
the terrestrial biosphere contributes to the atmospheric (CO2)-13/12CO2 variability but is unlikely to explain the full atmospheric C-13 signal.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we need to better constrain the C-13 budget of the terrestrial biosphere, in particular the disequilibrium flux, in order to better understand the C-13 dynamics of the atmosphere and to better partition the atmospheric carbon sink into its terrestrial and oceanic components.

, although the terrestrial C-13 disequilibrium flux may be the main contributor to IAV in atmospheric (CO2)-13CO(2) ratios, the current understanding of the processes that control this flux is still too uncertain to allow for a reliable partitioning of the total carbon sink.
the atmospheric C-12 and (C-13) budgets are not in equilibrium and that the disequilibrium flux must be taken into account to correctly interpret the atmospheric C-2 and C-13 signals.
